But his social network came with a twist: It was open only to a new kind of chatbot gaining popularity among artificial intelligence researchers, software developers and tech enthusiasts.In just two days, more than 10,000 “Moltbots” were chatting with one another on the site, as their creators looked on with a mix of admiration, amusement and dread. Other tech enthusiasts flocked to Moltbook, just to watch the automated conversations on their computer screens.The chatty bots became the talk of Silicon Valley and an elaborate Rorschach test for belief in the current state of A.I. According to countless posts on the internet and myriad interviews with The New York Times, many saw a technology that could make their lives easier. Others saw more of the A.I. slop that has been filling the internet in recent months. And some saw the early signs of bots conspiring against their creators.“People are seeing what they expect to see, much like that famous psychological test where you stare at an ink blot,” said Perry Metzger, a technology consultant and entrepreneur who has closely tracked the rise of A.I. for decades.As the bots discussed everything from private email protocols to cryptocurrency sales to the nature of consciousness, much of what they said was nonsense. And some of their chatter was probably fed to them by their creators. But the bots were remarkably convincing as they seemed to discuss their own technical skills, their view of the world and their plans for the future.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. extractedText: NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market roared back on Friday, as technology stocks recovered much of their losses from earlier in the week and bitcoin halted its plunge, at least for now.The S&P 500 rallied 2% for its best day since May. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,206 points, or 2.5%, and topped the 50,000 level for the first time, while the Nasdaq composite leaped 2.2%.Chip companies helped drive the widespread rally, and Nvidia jumped 7.8% to trim its loss for the week, which came into the day at just over 10%. Broadcom climbed 7.1% and erased its drop for the week.They were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500, and they benefited from hopes for continued spending by customers diving into artificial-intelligence technology. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, for example, said late Thursday it expects to spend about $200 billion on investments this year to take advantage of “seminal opportunities like AI, chips, robotics, and low earth orbit satellites.”Such immense spending, similar to what Alphabet announced a day earlier, is creating concerns of its own, though. The question is whether all those dollars will create big enough profits to make the investments worth it. With doubt remaining about that, Amazon’s stock dropped 5.6%.Even with Friday’s surge, the S&P 500 still fell to its third losing week in the last four. Besides worries about spending by Big Tech companies, which are Wall Street’s most influential stocks, concerns about AI potentially stealing customers from software companies also hurt the market. Software stocks got hit particularly hard after AI firm Anthropic released free tools to automate things like legal services.Bitcoin, meanwhile, steadied following a weekslong plunge that had sent it more than halfway below its record price set in October. It climbed back above $70,000 after briefly dropping close to $60,000 late Thursday.Prices in the metals market also calmed a bit following their own wild swings. Gold rose 1.8% to settle at $4,979.80 per ounce, while silver added 0.2%.Their prices suddenly ran out of momentum last week following jaw-dropping rallies, which were driven by investors clamoring for something safe to own amid worries about political turmoil, a U.S. stock market that critics called expensive and huge debt loads for governments worldwide. By January, prices for gold and silver were surging so quickly that critics called it unsustainable.A board above the trading floor of the New York Stock displays the Dow Jones industrial average intra-day number as tops the 50,000 level for the first time, Friday, Feb. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Richard Drew)On Wall Street, the recovery for bitcoin helped stocks of companies enmeshed in the crypto economy. Robinhood Markets jumped 14% for the biggest gain in the S&P 500. Crypto trading platform Coinbase Global rose 13%. Strategy, the company that’s made a business of buying and holding bitcoin, soared 26.1%.Stocks of smaller U.S. companies also helped lead the market, along with companies whose profits depend on U.S. households spending more money. They benefited from potentially encouraging data on how U.S. consumers are feeling.A preliminary report from the University of Michigan suggested sentiment among U.S. consumers is improving slightly, when economists were expecting to see a drop. The improvement was strongest among households that own stocks, which are benefiting from the S&P 500 setting a record late last month.To be sure, sentiment “remained at dismal levels for consumers without stock holdings,” according to Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsu.Airline stocks strengthened with hopes that more confidence among U.S. households will translate into more spending on trips. That included gains of 9.3% for United Airlines, 8% for Delta Air Lines and 7.6% for American Airlines.The smaller stocks in the Russell 2000 index jumped 3.6%, well above the S&P 500’s gain. Smaller companies’ profits can be more dependent on the strength of the U.S. economy than those for big, multinational rivals.All told, the S&P 500 jumped 133.90 points to 6,932.30. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,206.95 to 50,115.67, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 490.63 to 23,031.21.In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe.That was even though Stellantis, the auto giant whose stock trades in Italy, lost a quarter of its value after saying it would take a charge of 22 billion euros, or $26 billion, as it dials back its electric vehicle production. # Intelligenza Artificiale: nel 2026 il 94% dei CEO manterrà gli investimenti anche senza ROI immediato

Press Release

2026年1月23日

[SCARICA IL REPORT](https://www.bcg.com/ja-jp/publications/2026/as-ai-investments-surge-ceos-take-the-lead)

**Milano—**L’**intelligenza artificiale** non è più soltanto un tema tecnologico, ma una **leva strategica centrale per la competitività delle imprese a livello globale**. Le aziende sono oggi pronte ad **accelerare e raddoppiare gli investimenti in AI entro il 2026**, confermando un cambio di paradigma ormai strutturale.

Secondo il
[***BCG AI Radar 2026***](https://www.bcg.com/ja-jp/publications/2026/as-ai-investments-surge-ceos-take-the-lead)
**, il terzo studio annuale di Boston Consulting Group (BCG)** sullo stato globale dell’intelligenza artificiale, le imprese investiranno in media **l’1,7% dei ricavi in AI nel corso dell’anno**, più del doppio rispetto al 2025. Una crescita che **non mostra segnali di rallentamento né ripensamenti**: il **94% delle aziende continuerà a investire in AI anche in assenza di ritorni finanziari immediati nel breve periodo**, riconoscendone il valore strategico di lungo termine.

Basata su un’indagine condotta su 2.360 top manager in 16 Paesi, tra cui 100 executive italiani e 640 CEO a livello globale, la ricerca mostra come l’AI stia rapidamente passando da iniziativa guidata dai CIO a priorità strategica presidiata direttamente dagli amministratori delegati. **Il 72% dei CEO dichiara, infatti, di essere il principale decision maker sull’intelligenza artificiale**, una quota più che raddoppiata rispetto allo scorso anno, **un CEO su due (50%)** afferma che la propria **stabilità professionale dipende dalla capacità di trasformare l’AI in risultati concreti per il business**.

In **Europa**, dove il **61% dei CEO** si dichiara fiducioso nella capacità dell’**Intelligenza Artificiale (AI)** di generare valore per il business, la trasformazione è già in pieno corso. Rispetto ad altre aree geografiche come **Asia e India**, però, le imprese europee mostrano una maggiore attenzione alla **gestione del rischio**, alla **sicurezza** e alla **compliance normativa**, elementi che stanno influenzando il ritmo e le modalità di adozione dell’AI.

Le aziende europee, incluse quelle **italiane**, investono sempre più nell’AI non solo per evitare di perdere competitività, ma perché ne riconoscono il **valore strategico nel ridisegnare i processi core**, i **modelli operativi** e intere **catene del valore**. L’Intelligenza Artificiale diventa così un abilitatore chiave della trasformazione aziendale di lungo periodo.

### AI agent: il nuovo motore di valore per le imprese

Uno dei principali **driver di fiducia nell’AI** è rappresentato dagli **AI agent**, sistemi intelligenti in grado di operare in modo sempre più **autonomo lungo interi processi aziendali**, dalla pianificazione all’esecuzione. Gli agenti AI stanno rapidamente passando da sperimentazioni isolate a componenti strutturali dei modelli operativi delle imprese.

extractedText: This performance arrives as the company seeks to list on the NSE SME platform. The offering comprises a fresh issue of shares valued at ₹71.85 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of ₹16.17 crore. Despite the robust top-line expansion, the lack of investor enthusiasm in the unofficial market points toward deeper questions regarding the company's valuation and its ability to expand profitability in a competitive sector. The Valuation Question CKK Retail Mart has priced its IPO in a band of ₹155 to ₹163 per share. Based on its FY25 profit after tax of ₹16.36 crore, the company is seeking a post-issue price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple in the vicinity of 20x. While its revenue grew significantly, a closer look at the financials reveals that key profitability metrics, such as EBITDA and net profit margins, were almost identical to the previous fiscal year, hovering around 7.5% and 5.4% respectively. This lack of margin expansion, coupled with a flat grey market premium where shares trade at the upper issue price, suggests that investors may perceive the IPO as fully valued, leaving little on the table for listing gains. Sector Headwinds and Peer Context The muted market sentiment is also contextualized by the broader environment for SME public offerings, which has seen increased investor scrutiny in early 2026 after a frenetic 2025. CKK operates in the high-volume, low-margin agro-commodity distribution space, a sector inherently sensitive to price volatility of raw materials and intense competition. While a direct comparison to large-cap giants like Adani Wilmar is inexact, the valuation sought by CKK is comparable to other small and mid-sized players in the distribution segment. This places the onus on the company to effectively deploy its IPO proceeds to generate superior returns in a challenging industry. Capital Allocation and Forward Path The company's proposed use of funds provides a clear roadmap for its immediate priorities. A substantial portion of the net proceeds, ₹43 crore, is allocated for working capital, which is critical for scaling its distribution network. A further ₹10.2 crore is earmarked for acquiring leasehold plots, with ₹1.9 crore dedicated to refurbishing existing warehouses. This strategy indicates a focus on strengthening its core operational infrastructure and logistical capabilities. The subscription window for the IPO will close on February 3, 2026, with the shares anticipated to begin trading on the NSE SME platform on February 6, 2026, which will serve as the first market-based verdict on its growth and valuation narrative.

# How a Headless CMS Scales Ecommerce Brands and Buying Experiences

![bracket tree with eight boxes in front of black and green background](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0817/7988/4088/articles/headlessCMS.png?v=1770266721&originalWidth=1848&originalHeight=782)

The platform built for future-proofing

As ecommerce brands grow, keeping content consistent across every channel gets harder. Today’s online buyers expect what McKinsey calls a “[zero difference](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/retail/our-insights/the-five-zeros-reshaping-stores)” experience.

That means no matter where they interact with your business, the brand should feel the same. Visuals, messaging, pricing, and product availability need to be consistent across every channel, from a mobile app to an in-store display. This level of consistency builds trust, loyalty, and ultimately, revenue.

But delivering that consistency becomes harder as customer touchpoints multiply. Today’s [B2B customers use an average of 10 interaction channels](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/five-fundamental-truths-how-b2b-winners-go-to-market-infographic) in their buying journey, up from five in 2016. More than 50% say they are likely to switch suppliers if they don’t have a smooth experience across channels.

Growing brands often start with a [traditional content management system (CMS)](/blog/ecommerce-cms) like WordPress or Drupal, but may discover they can’t support omnichannel complexity at scale. That’s where modern [headless CMS platforms](/enterprise/blog/headless-cms), like Sanity, Contentful, and Contentstack, come into play. Built for flexibility and scale, these platforms allow ecommerce teams to create content once, manage it centrally, and deliver it everywhere through APIs.

That’s why more enterprise brands are adopting [headless architectures](/enterprise/blog/headless-architecture) to unify content and commerce. By separating the front end from the back end, teams can integrate a headless CMS into their stack without rebuilding their ecommerce foundation. This approach keeps content and product data aligned, up to date, and ready to deliver personalized experiences across any channel.

In this article, we explore how to build a headless ecommerce stack that integrates seamlessly with a modern CMS. We also show how this approach unlocks speed, scale, and smarter omnichannel delivery.

## Traditional CMS vs. headless CMS: Key differences for ecommerce brands

Traditional CMS platforms such as Drupal or Adobe Experience Manager were originally designed to help teams build and manage websites without needing significant developer support. They work well for publishing content to a single website.

But these platforms weren’t designed for omnichannel content distribution. They often struggle to support delivery across touchpoints like social media, in-store displays, mobile apps, or email campaigns. As a result, they rarely provide the flexibility or performance needed to support ecommerce at scale.

Headless CMS platforms, on the other hand, are API-first systems. This means that how content is created and stored (the “body”), can easily be separated from where it’s displayed (the “head”). This separation allows brands to deliver content across any channel through APIs.

For large ecommerce brands, headless CMS platforms act as centralized content hubs. They make it easy for teams across the business to create and publish on-brand content across websites, emails, social posts, product pages, and more. Just as important, they integrate smoothly into headless ecommerce stacks, helping brands streamline operations and deliver fast, cohesive customer experiences.

### Content management workflows and team collaboration

Traditional CMS platforms can centralize website content, but they aren’t really designed to manage and distribute content across multiple channels. Without a unified system that spans ecommerce, social media, email, and other touchpoints, content workflows become fragmented and difficult to coordinate. Teams end up working in separate systems and manually applying brand guidelines in each one. This can easily lead to inaccurate product information, disjointed brand messaging, and haphazard campaign execution.

A headless CMS offers stronger support for omnichannel marketing. By centralizing content in a single system, a headless CMS allows cross-functional teams to collaborate more effectively. Everyone works from the same platform, with shared access to approved assets and templates. extractedText: Modern RoddingSpecial Features - MR Parting Shot: He was Ed Iskenderian, but Everyone Called Him “Isky” February 5, 2026 There isn’t a hot rodder alive who hasn’t felt the “ear-to-ear” smile when behind the wheel, especially a roadster. Isky was no different, but he might have been the “first” to experience the pure joy of driving a hot rod. By Brian Brennan – Photography By the Author, Matt Stone & the Ed Iskenderian Collection Ed “Isky” Iskenderian, who died on February 3, 2026, at the age 104, was a true hot rod pioneer known for speed, craftsmanship, and endless curiosity. Born in 1921, Isky grew up in Southern California during the early, hungry days after the Depression, when ambitious young people repurposed whatever they could to chase the thrill of speed. He once recalled that Model Ts and As—cheap, plentiful, and slow—started as raw material for ambitious kids who wanted more but had little money. “We were kids in the postwar era,” he said, “and we bought used cars for $5 or $10 and tried to figure out how to make them go faster without spending what we didn’t have.” During the heyday years of Isky the company, you could find Isky, the man, at work daily and behind the counter to help any hot rodder achieve his “need for speed.” If Isky’s legend is anchored in a single car, it is the roadster that bears his name—the Isky roadster. Its evolution began with a car owned by his lifelong friend John Athan, but the real transformation came from Isky’s hands and mind. Built on late 1920s Essex framerails, the car combined a 1923 Model T body with a Ford B Flathead engine, initially tuned and modified in ways that reflected a teenager’s relentless experimentation. The chassis was upgraded with a 1932 Ford front axle and brakes, and the driving experience was electrified by a then-cutting-edge mix of components from around the automotive world. A distinctive Auburn instrument panel and a two-piece Pontiac grille shell—sourced from junkyards and rebuilt into a unique, aerodynamic front end—gave the car its unmistakable look. It was much later in his life, but he never passed up the chance to attend an event or visit the dry lakes where his speed quest began—and, of course, behind the wheel of his roadster. Isky’s early innovations went beyond just the bodywork. He combined a mix of speed parts and homebuilt solutions: a Franklin front axle and air-cooled Franklin steering, a Ruckstell two-speed rearend, and Western Auto Center “air-cooled” tires that were more about brand-name bravado than actual cooling. He experimented with multiple V-8s, ultimately choosing a 1932 Ford Flathead with a three-speed transmission as the core of the roadster’s performance. The engine was a focal point: Isky designed and tested various intake manifolds and carburetor setups, from a homemade four-carburetor intake to later combinations using Navarro and Edelbrock parts. Throughout these trials, his approach mixed practical engineering with a sense of artistry—shown in the hand-fabricated aluminum valve covers bearing his name in a cursive script, crafted with help from his friend Athan. His desk didn’t change much in appearance over the years, nor did the cigar—always in his hand and ready to enjoy life—which was made up of Isky Racing Cams, the business, and a good cigar. The roadster’s performance was about more than just speed—it served as a vehicle for learning. Isky’s road trip to Mexico in 1940, before his wartime service, highlighted the car’s durability and the driver’s composure under difficult road conditions. An “eyes wide open” moment during a test run near the Muroc Dry Lakes emphasized the dangers inherent in early hot rodding, but Isky’s calmness under pressure helped him survive and continue improving the machine. Bobby Meeks (left) with Isky posing for a photo while running a Ford Flathead on the dyno. Isky knew cams, but he truly knew how to tune an engine, and his carburetor work was also legendary. Isky recalls the somewhat tense ride, one that makes you pucker up; he and Athan took it to the Muroc Dry Lakes to test the new engine and some modifications. When installing the 1932 Ford axle and brakes previously, Athan chose to modify the axle and frame to accommodate semi-elliptical springs instead of the stock transverse-leaf setup. Athan created a set of pad-like mounting brackets to adapt these springs to his frame and axle, but they were brazed onto the front of the car rather than welded with more robust steel-to-steel fusing. Before their trip to the dry lakes, Isky noticed that some of the brazing had started to crack, but “hadn’t spread too far.” It was June 1948 when Isky, along with his roadster, appeared on the cover of Hot Rod. It was the early days for car magazines, camshaft companies, and the world of hot rodding, and Isky was there for all of it.
